newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee higher, supply improves.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee higher, supply improves.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices were higher on Monday in line with marginal gains in London last week, with values seen keeping steady despite improving supply, traders said.
They said the local price was quoted at 3,300-3,350 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with 3,200-3,250 rupiah a week ago.
The export price was quoted at $1,410-$1,425/tonne FOB Lampung, down from $1,400-$1,450 last Monday.
"The market has been generally quiet because of the Easter holidays," one trader said.

"But there were some players who have been buying actively, building up their stocks," he said. "Although local prices are high compared with export prices, they have been buying in anticipation of prices improving at the terminals."
London Robusta futures ended narrowly mixed last Thursday in sluggish pre-Easter holiday trading, but the benchmark May contract closed $2 higher at $1,632 per tonne.

After the New York market closed last Wednesday, the Association of Coffee Producing Countries said in a report the supply prospects in the third quarter of 1997 continued to look tight and could be vulnerable to price disruptions.

The London-based ACPC lowered its estimate for the Central American 1996/97 crop to 15.4 million bags from its previous forecast of 15.8 million bags. It lowered world consumption to 76 million bags on an annualised basis from its previous forecast of 76.5 million bags.
Indonesian traders said they did not expect any significant changes to the global robusta supply situation.
"The robusta picture seems to be pretty clear at this stage," one trader said. "I expect output in the Ivory Coast to increase, but not significantly."
"In the case of Indonesia, production is expected to be lower by about 20 percent," he said.

He said expectations of a smaller Indonesian crop seemed to have been taken in stride by traders in London, adding that any change in their buying pattern was only likely to emerge when the markets begin to feel the squeeze.

"From the buyers' point of view, I think they feel it (the possible decline in output) is only rumours," he said. "Only when the market feels the effects of the lower production will the traders begin to take action."
Speculation has been rife in Indonesia that the country's crop could decline by up to 20 percent this year.
